source: derived from X.690 clause 8 and the ISP1 figure 3-3 layout
note: The BER primitives and the ISP1 transport mapping layer framing that SLE is built on. These are the foundation the operation encodings sit on, so they are pinned first: a wrong INTEGER length or length-form boundary corrupts every operation above it. The association state machine and the operation encodings are not covered here.

encode.name: integer-zero
encode.note: BER INTEGER zero: tag 0x02, length 1, content 0x00. Zero still takes a content octet; a zero-length INTEGER is not valid BER.

encode.name: integer-127-fits-one-octet
encode.note: 127 is the largest value one content octet holds, because BER INTEGER is two's-complement and a leading 0x80 would read as negative. Content 0x7f.

encode.name: integer-128-needs-a-leading-zero
encode.note: 128 needs two content octets: 0x00 0x80. Without the leading zero the 0x80 would decode as -128. This is the single most common BER INTEGER mistake, so it is pinned next to its 127 neighbour.

encode.name: integer-minus-one
encode.note: -1 is 0xff in one octet. Paired with integer-255 below, which is 0x00 0xff, this pins the sign handling in both directions.

encode.name: integer-255-needs-a-leading-zero
encode.note: 255 is 0x00 0xff in two octets, distinct from -1 which is 0xff in one.

encode.name: integer-minus-128-fits-one-octet
encode.note: -128 fits one octet as 0x80, since two's-complement reaches -128 in eight bits. An encoder using a non-minimal length would write 0xff 0x80 here.

encode.name: integer-minus-129-needs-two-octets
encode.note: -129 is one past what one octet holds, giving 0xff 0x7f.

encode.name: octet-string-empty
encode.note: An empty OCTET STRING: tag 0x04, length 0, no content.

encode.name: octet-string-ascii
encode.note: The ASCII 'astro' as an OCTET STRING: tag 0x04, length 5, then the octets.

encode.name: null
encode.note: NULL is tag 0x05 with a zero length and no content.

encode.name: sequence-empty
encode.note: An empty SEQUENCE: constructed tag 0x30, length 0.

encode.name: sequence-containing-an-integer
encode.note: A SEQUENCE wrapping INTEGER 1: tag 0x30, length 3, then 02 01 01. The length counts the encoded element, not the value.

encode.name: length-127-short-form
encode.note: Lengths up to 127 use the short form: a single octet holding the length. 127 is 0x7f, the largest short form.

encode.name: length-128-long-form
encode.note: 128 needs the long form: 0x81 says one length octet follows, then 0x80. The 0x80 bit of the first octet is what distinguishes the two forms.

encode.name: tml-heartbeat
encode.note: An ISP1 TML heartbeat: message type 3, three reserved zero octets, a four-octet body length of zero, and no body. Eight octets total. The three reserved octets must be zero and a receiver that skipped them would read the length four octets early.

encode.name: tml-pdu-message
encode.note: A TML message carrying an SLE PDU: type 1, reserved zeros, body length 3, then the body 02 01 ff (a BER INTEGER -1). The body length is big-endian across four octets.

encode.name: tml-context-message
encode.note: A context message body is fixed at 12 octets by clause 3.3.2.2.4, unlike a PDU body which is variable. It opens with the protocol identification 'ISP1' (49 53 50 31), then the version, then the heartbeat interval and dead factor as big-endian integers (clause 3.3.2.2.6). Here version 1, interval 30 seconds, dead factor 3.

reject.name: tml-shorter-than-the-eight-octet-header
reject.note: A TML message is at least eight octets: type, three reserved, and a four-octet length.

reject.name: tml-body-shorter-than-its-declared-length
reject.note: The length field says four body octets but only two follow. A decoder must refuse rather than return a short body.

reject.name: tml-context-body-not-twelve-octets
reject.note: A context message body is exactly 12 octets. Four is refused at construction rather than sent, because a peer reads the body by position and cannot tell a short one from data.

reject.name: tml-heartbeat-with-a-body
reject.note: A heartbeat carries no body at all. Anything in it is refused, since a peer expecting an empty body would treat the octets as the start of the next message.
